text: Your baby may start pulling up to stand using furniture. Place sturdy items nearby so they can practice safely.
Waving bye-bye, clapping, and pointing are all signs your baby is developing important social communication skills.
Try stacking two or three blocks together and letting your baby knock them down. This teaches cause and effect while building hand-eye coordination.
Your baby may start cruising along furniture between 9 and 12 months. Rearrange seating so they can move from one piece to the next.
Responding to their own name consistently is a milestone around this age. Use their name often during play and mealtimes.
Your baby is learning object permanence. Play peek-a-boo or hide a toy under a blanket and watch them look for it.
Babbling with consonant sounds like "mama" and "dada" is your baby experimenting with language. Repeat their sounds back to encourage more.
Let your baby practice picking up small, safe foods with a pincer grasp. This fine motor skill develops rapidly between 9 and 12 months.
Your baby may start understanding simple instructions like "give me the ball." Use short, clear phrases and gentle gestures together.
Banging two objects together is a sign of growing coordination and curiosity. Offer wooden spoons, cups, or soft blocks for this purpose.
Your baby may show stranger anxiety around this age. This is a healthy sign of strong attachment to you.
Try reading board books together and letting your baby turn the pages. They are building early literacy skills even before they understand the words.
Pointing at objects they want is one of the first intentional communication gestures. Acknowledge what they point to by naming it.
Your baby may start imitating simple actions like stirring a spoon or brushing hair. This imitation play is how they learn about daily life.
Some babies take their first steps around 12 months, but many don't walk until later. Both timelines are perfectly normal.
Closer to 12 months, some babies start resisting their morning nap. If this happens consistently, try gradually pushing the morning nap later rather than dropping it right away.
Separation anxiety can cause nighttime wake-ups around 9-10 months. A brief, calm reassurance visit is more helpful than changing the whole routine.
Keep the sleep environment dark, cool, and quiet. A white noise machine at a moderate volume can help your baby sleep more soundly.
A short, predictable bedtime routine of 15-20 minutes signals to your baby that sleep is coming. Bath, book, song, and bed works well.
Your baby should still sleep on their back on a firm, flat surface. Remove all loose blankets, pillows, and stuffed animals from the crib.
Night weaning often happens naturally between 9-12 months as your baby eats more solids during the day. Talk to your pediatrician if you are unsure.
If your baby pulls to stand in the crib and cries, they may need help learning to sit back down. Practice this skill during daytime play.
Aim for wake windows of 2.5-3.5 hours between naps at this age. Overtired babies often have a harder time falling asleep.
Early morning waking before 6 AM is common at this age. Ensure the room is very dark and avoid stimulating activities if they wake too early.
Teething discomfort can disrupt sleep. If your baby seems in pain, ask your pediatrician about age-appropriate pain relief before bed.
Travel and schedule changes can temporarily affect sleep. Be patient and return to your normal routine as soon as possible.
If your baby is on two naps, the first nap is usually around 9-10 AM and the second around 1-2 PM. Adjust based on your baby's sleepy cues.
Some babies experience a sleep regression around 10-12 months tied to developmental leaps like standing and cruising. It usually passes within 2-4 weeks.
By 9-12 months, your baby can enjoy a wide variety of soft finger foods. Cut everything into small, manageable pieces about the size of a pea.
Offer water in an open cup or straw cup during meals. Practicing now helps them transition off bottles by 12-15 months.
Your baby still needs breast milk or formula as their primary nutrition until 12 months. Solids are complementary at this stage.
It can take 10-15 exposures to a new food before a baby accepts it. Keep offering without pressure if they reject something.
Iron-rich foods like fortified cereal, pureed meats, beans, and lentils are especially important between 9 and 12 months as iron stores from birth deplete.
Let your baby self-feed as much as possible. The mess is worth it for developing independence and fine motor skills.
Avoid honey until after 12 months due to the risk of infant botulism. This applies to all forms including baked goods made with honey.
Gagging is different from choking and is a normal protective reflex as your baby learns to manage new textures. Stay calm and let them work through it.
Offer three meals and 1-2 snacks per day alongside breast milk or formula. Follow your baby's hunger and fullness cues.
Introduce common allergens like peanut butter (thinned or in puffs), egg, and dairy early and often. Research shows this can reduce allergy risk.
Avoid added sugar and salt in your baby's food. Their kidneys and taste buds are still developing, and whole foods provide everything they need.
If your baby turns their head away or closes their mouth, they are telling you they are done. Respect these fullness cues to build a healthy relationship with food.
Eating together as a family helps your baby learn by watching you. They are more likely to try new foods when they see you enjoying them.
Soft fruits like banana, ripe avocado, and steamed pear are great starter finger foods. Mash them lightly or cut into small strips.
If you are planning to wean from breastfeeding, dropping one feeding at a time over several weeks is gentler for both you and your baby.
Regular well-child visits include developmental screening and a check on growth. Bring any questions you have been saving up.
Talk to your pediatrician about which vaccines are due during this stage. Staying on schedule with immunizations is important for protecting your growing explorer.
Teething often intensifies between 9 and 12 months as more teeth come in. A chilled (not frozen) teething ring can provide soothing relief.
Your baby's first dental visit should happen by their first birthday or within six months of their first tooth erupting.
Ear infections are common at this age. Watch for ear tugging, fussiness, trouble sleeping, or fever, and contact your pediatrician if you suspect one.
Once teeth appear, brush them twice daily with a rice-grain-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste and a soft infant toothbrush.
Frequent hand washing is one of the best ways to prevent illness as your baby explores more surfaces and objects.
If your baby gets a mild cold, saline drops and a bulb syringe can help clear nasal congestion. A cool-mist humidifier in the bedroom helps too.
Keep your baby's immunization records in one place. You will need them for daycare enrollment and future doctor visits.
Mild side effects after vaccines, like low fever or fussiness for a day or two, are normal and a sign the immune system is responding.
Flat feet are completely normal at this age. The arch develops over the first few years and usually does not need any intervention.
If your baby has persistent diaper rash that does not improve with barrier cream, it could be a yeast infection. Ask your pediatrician about treatment.
The flu vaccine is recommended annually starting at 6 months. If your baby has not had one yet, it is not too late to catch up.
Fill a container with large, soft items and let your baby practice taking things out and putting them back in. This builds problem-solving skills.
Try a simple treasure basket with safe household items of different textures, shapes, and weights. Your baby will love exploring each one.
Roll a ball back and forth with your baby. This early turn-taking game teaches social interaction and tracking moving objects.
Let your baby play with water during bath time using cups and containers for pouring. Supervised water play is great for sensory development.
Create a simple obstacle course with couch cushions on the floor. Crawling over and around them builds core strength and spatial awareness.
Sing songs with hand motions like "Itsy Bitsy Spider" or "Pat-a-Cake." Your baby is learning to connect words with actions.
Offer large crayons and paper for first scribbling experiences. Hold the crayon together if needed and celebrate any marks they make.
Play music and dance together. Moving to rhythm supports motor development and is a joyful bonding experience.
Take your baby outside to feel grass, leaves, and sand. Outdoor sensory experiences are rich learning opportunities.
Nesting cups or stacking rings teach your baby about size relationships. Show them how to stack, then let them explore on their own.
Play "Where did it go?" by hiding a toy under one of two cups. This strengthens memory and problem-solving abilities.
Let your baby bang on pots, pans, and wooden spoons. Making noise teaches cause and effect and is endlessly entertaining for them.
Narrate what you are doing throughout the day. "Now we are washing your hands" builds vocabulary even before your baby speaks.
Try supervised play with safe kitchen items like measuring cups, silicone spatulas, and plastic bowls. Real objects fascinate babies at this age.
Push toys with handles encourage walking practice and build confidence in new walkers. Let your baby push at their own pace.
Now that your baby is mobile, secure all furniture to the wall with anti-tip brackets. Dressers and bookshelves are the most common tipping hazards.
Keep all small objects, coins, and button batteries out of reach. Anything that fits through a toilet paper roll is a choking hazard.
Install safety gates at the top and bottom of stairs. Pressure-mounted gates are fine at the bottom, but use hardware-mounted gates at the top.

Check that your baby's car seat is rear-facing and properly installed. Safety experts recommend keeping children rear-facing as long as possible, until they reach the seat's maximum height or weight limit.
Never leave your baby unattended near water, even for a moment. Drowning can happen in as little as {{1 inch|2.5 cm}} of water.
Cover all electrical outlets with safety covers or plates. Crawling babies are naturally drawn to outlets at their eye level.
Move cleaning products, medications, and chemicals to high, locked cabinets. Use child-proof locks on any low cabinets that contain hazards.
Cut round foods like grapes, cherry tomatoes, and hot dogs lengthwise into small pieces. Round shapes are the most common choking hazard for babies.
Set your water heater to {{120°F|49°C}} or below to prevent scalding. Always test bath water with your wrist or elbow before placing your baby in.
Keep blind cords and curtain strings out of reach or switch to cordless window coverings. These are a serious strangulation hazard.
Lower the crib mattress to its lowest setting once your baby can pull to stand. This prevents them from climbing or falling out.
Save your local poison control number in your phone. Fast access matters in an emergency.
Avoid walkers with wheels, as pediatric safety experts warn they contribute to injuries and do not help babies learn to walk.
Use corner guards on sharp furniture edges like coffee tables and fireplace hearths. New cruisers fall frequently and at head height.
Always supervise your baby while eating. Stay within arm's reach and learn infant CPR so you are prepared if choking occurs.
Your baby may start using one or two real words with meaning around this age. Celebrate every attempt at communication, even if the word isn't quite right.
Offering your baby a shape sorter or puzzle with large knobs helps them learn about matching and spatial relationships through trial and error.
Your baby may hand you a book when they want to be read to. Following their lead and reading what interests them builds a lifelong love of books.
Try giving simple one-step directions paired with a gesture, like holding out your hand and saying "give me the ball." Your baby is learning to connect your words with actions.
Your baby is beginning to understand that objects have names. Labeling everything around them — "that's a tree," "there's a bird" — fuels their growing vocabulary.
Around 12 months or later, some babies begin transitioning from two naps to one. If this happens, expect a few weeks of inconsistency where some days need two naps and others just one.
If your baby is dropping to one nap around 12 months or later, aim for a midday nap around 12-1 PM. An earlier bedtime can bridge the gap while they adjust.
If your baby has started climbing out of the crib, lower the mattress to the floor setting and remove anything they could use as a stepping stool.
Resist the urge to skip naps for outings. Consistent daytime sleep actually leads to better nighttime sleep and a happier baby overall.
If bedtime tantrums start, a simple countdown routine can help. "Two more minutes of play, then we brush teeth" gives your baby a sense of what's coming.

As your baby approaches their first birthday, you can begin introducing whole cow's milk as a drink. Aim for about {{16-24 ounces|475-710 ml}} per day -- too much can fill them up and crowd out solid foods.
Try offering a dipping sauce like hummus or yogurt alongside finger foods. Dipping is fun for your baby and can make unfamiliar foods more appealing.
If your baby insists on feeding themselves, let them. Offer a pre-loaded spoon so they practice, and eat alongside them to model how it's done.
When the time feels right, start transitioning away from bottles. Offering milk in a cup at mealtimes and water between meals makes the switch easier.
Don't worry if your baby's appetite fluctuates day to day. Growth spurts, teething, and activity levels all affect hunger. Trust their cues.
Walking on tiptoes occasionally is common as your baby experiments with movement. If it becomes their primary walking pattern, mention it to your pediatrician.
If your baby develops a rash after trying a new food, note what they ate and when the rash appeared. Share this with your pediatrician to help identify any food sensitivities.
Diarrhea from stomach bugs can dehydrate babies quickly. Offer small, frequent sips of an oral rehydration solution and contact your pediatrician if it lasts more than a day.
As your baby starts walking, expect bruises on shins and foreheads from tumbles. This is a normal part of learning, but always rule out head injuries after harder falls.
Try giving your baby a toy with doors, latches, or zippers to open and close. These fine motor challenges keep them engaged and build dexterity.
Set up a low shelf with a few rotating toys rather than a big toy box. Fewer choices at once help your baby focus and play more deeply with each toy.
Your baby may start pretend play, like feeding a stuffed animal or putting a doll to bed. Join in and expand on their ideas to encourage imagination.
Try blowing bubbles and letting your baby chase and pop them. It's great for visual tracking, reaching, and getting those new walkers moving.
As your baby starts walking, shoes with flexible, non-slip soles protect their feet outdoors. Indoors, bare feet or grip socks are best for balance.
Keep laundry detergent pods locked away. Their bright colors attract babies, and biting into one can cause serious chemical burns to the mouth and throat.
Check that your baby's toys don't have small parts that can break off. Regularly inspect toys for cracks, loose pieces, or peeling paint.
If you have a fireplace or space heater, use a safety screen or barrier. Even warm surfaces can burn a baby's sensitive skin on contact.
Keep an eye on older children's snacks around your baby. Popcorn, nuts, hard candy, and gum are choking hazards that are easy to overlook when siblings share.
